newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Creditanstalt tender closes, no info on bidders.
newsitem.headline: Creditanstalt tender closes, no info on bidders.

text.p: The latest tender for Austrian selloff candidate Creditanstalt-Bankverein closes on Friday, but sources near to the government said it was unlikely that information on potential bidders would be released before next week.
"Nobody wants to have their weekend ruined," the source told Reuters. "I don't think (the government) will have an interest in releasing any information on this."
Finance Minister Viktor Klima, in charge of the sale, has indicated that up to five interested parties have asked for a copy of a detailed information memorandum on Creditanstalt.
Potential bidders have until midnight on Friday to submit an offer to JP Morgan, the government's adviser. A two- to three-week due diligence period is expected to start on Monday.
So far, only one consortium has confirmed its intention to make a binding offer.

The group, led by Austro-Italian insurer EA-Generali and including Germany's Commerzbank, Banca Commerciale Italiana and Austrian savings bank Die Erste, said on Thursday it would make a bid for a "substantial part" of the government's 70 percent voting stake in Austria's flagship bank.

The consortium -- excluding Die Erste -- in September made a bid for roughly half the stake, offering Klima about 6.7 billion schillings ($632 million), but was turned down because the government insisted it wanted to sell its 19.9 million share voting stake in the bank in its entirety.

Klima has indicated he will be more flexible this time around. According to unconfirmed media reports, the group is now poised to bid about 10 billion schillings for a large part of the share package, worth a total of about 14.6 billion schillings at current market prices.

A raft of suitors has come and gone since the bank was first put up for sale in late 1991, but they lost interest one after the other because of what they perceived as political bickering and a bias against foreigners in Austria.
Klima, eager for billions of schillings in revenue from the sale of the country's most traditional finance house, has said he wants to wrap up the sale before the end of the year.

Creditanstalt's preference shares have risen strongly over the past few days as investors sensed Austria's longest running privatisation project since World War Two may be coming to an end. The stock has gained 6.4 percent over the week to close at 517 schillings on Friday.
